question: A finance team's project instructions include a standing rule that every figure must be reported in euros, plus several directions that were only ever meant for individual past deliverables, and Claude's answers in the project have become inconsistent. Which two revisions would make those instructions work better as standing direction? Select two.
options: A) Rewrite each rule as a longer, more formal paragraph so none of them is overlooked.
B) Add a line at the top of the list telling Claude to follow every rule carefully.
C) Move the list out of the project and paste it into the first message of each chat.
D) Delete directions that were only ever meant for one particular past deliverable.
E) Give the reason behind the euro-only rule so Claude can apply it to new cases.
correct_answers: D) Delete directions that were only ever meant for one particular past deliverable.
E) Give the reason behind the euro-only rule so Claude can apply it to new cases.
explanations: Length and formality do not resolve which rules still apply. A long list of stale directions becomes a longer list of stale directions, and dense instructions are harder for the team to review.

A generic exhortation to follow the rules adds no information about which directions still apply or which take priority. Emphasis is not specification, and the outdated entries keep pulling answers in their own direction.

This gives up the main advantage of project instructions, which is that durable direction applies automatically to every chat. Pasted instructions have to be maintained by hand and will vary between chats and between people.

Correct. Standing instructions should hold for every chat in the project. One-off directions kept past their deliverable pull answers toward a job nobody is doing any more, which is a direct source of the inconsistency.

Correct, and for an unrelated reason: it improves a rule that stays rather than removing one that should go. Stating why figures must be in euros lets Claude extend the intent sensibly to situations the rule never named.
